title: Knowing without fixing
hook: you know an angry mind as angry: that is the whole instruction

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was citta, the mind, and your line was know the mind. Did you notice a worry that had gone quiet? Day two hundred fifty-nine, the end of another week in the sutta.

You notice you're anxious. Right away, a whole repair crew shows up. You should calm down. Why are you like this? Try breathing slower. Think positive. Fix it, fix it, fix it. And somehow, the anxiety gets worse, now with a layer of frustration on top: anxious, and anxious about being anxious. Yesterday's list in the sutta had an instruction hiding in it that's so simple it's easy to miss. Today: knowing without fixing.
screen: `THE REPAIR CREW SHOWS UP.` → `'JUST RELAX.'` → `AN INSTRUCTION HIDING IN PLAIN SIGHT.`

segments.voice: Look again at how the sutta words it. A mind with anger: know it as a mind with anger. That's all. It doesn't say, then remove the anger. It doesn't say, replace it with kindness. It doesn't say, feel bad for being angry. In this section, the whole instruction is to know. Other teachings in the Buddhist tradition do give remedies: kindness for ill will, reflection on the body for lust, and we'll meet those. But the Satipatthana Sutta puts something first. Before you change anything, see it clearly. Here's why that matters. The moment we try to fix a mind state, we're usually pushing against it, and pushing is its own kind of aversion. It's the second arrow again, aimed at our own moods. Knowing, on the other hand, takes a step back. When you say, this is an angry mind, there's no longer just anger. There's also a knowing of the anger. There's a little space there, and in that space the anger can loosen by itself, the way a knot loosens when you stop pulling both ends. Look back over this week and you'll see the same move everywhere. The parts of the body, sorted like grain. The elements, felt as they are. The charnel ground: this body too. Feelings: pleasant, painful, neither. The second arrow, not fired. The mind, known as the weather. Every one of them is seeing, not fixing. Six sections, one move.
screen: `A MIND WITH ANGER: KNOW IT.` · `SEE CLEARLY BEFORE CHANGING.` · `FIXING IS OFTEN PUSHING.` · `THE WEEK: SEEING, NOT FIXING.` · then, large: `JUST KNOW IT.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Find whatever mood is here right now: restless, flat, content, tired, a little sad. Name it plainly: a restless mind. Then, instead of fixing it, just stay with it, the way you'd sit with a friend who doesn't need advice. If the urge to fix it shows up, know that too: a mind that wants to fix. Nothing to do but know. The bell holds the time.
Knowing. In this section of the sutta, the whole instruction for a mind state, angry or calm, is simply to know it, nothing more.
Your line: just know it. Today, when a mood shows up, name it once, and hold off fixing it for one full breath. Day two hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Insight meditation teachers often stress bare knowing of mind states, noting 'angry' or 'restless' without judgment, as the first step; remedies such as loving-kindness are taught separately.

fork.setup: you sit to meditate and notice you're irritated. what does the sutta's instruction on the mind say to do first?
options: know it: this is an irritated mind.
stop meditating until the mood passes.
fork.reveal: the sutta says to know the mind as it is. seeing clearly comes before any change.

trapdoor: what you thought: knowing without fixing means giving up on getting better.
what it means: seeing a state clearly first, so it can loosen on its own.
what a scholar hears: MN 10's mind section contains no remedies; remedies for unwholesome thoughts appear elsewhere, for example in MN 20, the Vitakkasaṇṭhāna Sutta.
